chunks: My father (may God have mercy on him) narrated to us. He said: Sa'd ibn Abdullah narrated to us from Ayyub ibn Nuh from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr from Muthanna ibn al-Walid al-Hannat from Abu Basir. He said: Abu Abdullah al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) said to me:

Do you not become sad? Do you not worry? Do you not feel pain? I said: Of course, by God. He said: So when that happens to you, then remember death, your solitude in your grave, the streaming of your eyes onto your cheeks, the breaking of your joints, the worms eating your flesh, your afflictions, and your cutting off from this world; for indeed that prompts you to perform deeds and deters you from much of the greed over this world.

key_terms.الحرص على الدنيا: Greed over the world - excessive attachment to material life that remembrance of death counteracts
key_terms.الموت: Death - the central theme of contemplation prescribed as a spiritual remedy
key_terms.وحدتك في قبرك: Your solitude in your grave - the loneliness of the grave, where no worldly companion remains
key_terms.يحثك على العمل: Prompts you to perform deeds - the motivating effect of death contemplation on righteous action

ai.seo_question: What does Imam al-Sadiq say about remembering death as a remedy for worldly attachment?
ai.summary: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (AS) instructs his companion Abu Basir on a powerful spiritual practice: when experiencing sadness, worry, or pain, one should contemplate the realities of death and the grave. The Imam provides a vivid, unflinching description of what awaits in the grave — solitude, decomposition, worms consuming the flesh — not to create despair, but as a therapeutic antidote to worldly attachment. This teaching reflects a central ascetic tradition in Shia spirituality where meditation on death (dhikr al-mawt) is regarded as the most effective deterrent against excessive materialism and the strongest motivator for righteous action.
